conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a well-studied tool that helps us understand how moms are feeling emotionally in the weeks after birth, so we can be sure you’re getting whatever support you may need.

Everything we discuss stays confidential within your medical team, and this is a judgment-free space—there’s no right or wrong answer, only what’s true for you. We’ll go through 10 questions about how you’ve felt over the past seven days; each one is quick, and we’ll move at your pace.

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin:

1. Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things as much as you usually do?

[soft exhale]  
Honestly… not really. I’ll smile if someone makes a joke, but it feels kind of forced. I used to laugh a lot—my husband and I would watch silly shows every night—but lately it’s like the humor just bounces off me. Most of the time I’m too tired to find things funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[give a small shrug]  
I can still laugh, just… it’s not the same. It feels kind of distant, like I have to remind myself to enjoy the moment instead of just naturally laughing like I used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[pauses, eyes on the blanket]  
Not really. Even little things—like my favorite coffee or a walk—feel more like chores I *should* do than stuff I actually want. I keep telling myself, “It’ll be fun once I get there,” but I’m not… looking forward to anything the way I used to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[glances down, twisting the hospital band on my wrist]  
Yeah… mostly at night when the baby won’t settle. If he keeps crying I start thinking I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not feeding him right, or I missed some cue. My head knows it’s probably normal newborn stuff, but I still catch myself replaying the day and picking apart every little thing I did.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrapping the blanket tighter around my shoulders]  
Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there, baby’s asleep and the house is quiet, but my chest still feels tight—like I’m waiting for something bad to happen. Most of the worry is about him: is he breathing, is he getting enough milk, am I missing some sign he’s sick? There’s no real reason, but the thoughts just loop.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[hugging the blanket tighter, voice a little shaky]  
A couple of times, yeah. It’s usually when I’m alone with the baby—my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t catch my breath. Nothing’s actually wrong, but suddenly I’m sure something awful is about to happen. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and exhausted.
Things have been getting on top of me

[lets out a slow breath, eyes fixed on the floor]  
Yes… most days. It’s not that any single thing is huge—just feeding, changing, trying to sleep—but they pile up. I’ll be rocking the baby at 3 a.m. thinking, “How am I going to get through tomorrow?” I’m managing, but it feels like I’m barely one step ahead and could tumble any second.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[quiet for a second, rubbing the edge of the blanket]  
A few nights this week. I’ll finally get him down, but then I lie there staring at the ceiling, thoughts racing—mostly about whether I’m doing anything right. I wouldn’t say I’m super unhappy, just… keyed-up and heavy at the same time. Takes me a long time to drift off, and when I do I wake up at the slightest sound.
I have felt sad or miserable

[shrugs one shoulder, eyes glassy]  
Yeah… I guess I do feel sad some of the day. It’s not all the time, but it hits in waves—like when I’m feeding him and suddenly feel lonely or when I see other moms looking so put-together. I just feel… blah, like the color’s been turned down on everything.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[shakes head slowly]  
No… I haven’t actually cried. I feel teary sometimes—like there’s a lump in my throat—but the tears never come. It’s more this dull, heavy feeling than an actual cry.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly, eyes widening]  
No—never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and tired, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again and be okay for my baby.

You've shared how the joy that used to come easily-laughing at your favorite shows, looking forward to simple pleasures-now feels distant or forced. Daily waves of sadness, <sym>racing thoughts at night</sym>, and sudden <sym>panicky moments</sym> when you're alone with your baby leave you exhausted and wondering how you'll "get through tomorrow." You're working hard to meet your little one's needs while feeling you're "barely one step ahead," all without the support you hoped this season would bring.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 19, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished enjoyment and effortful laughter, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost no anticipatory enjoyment, describing even favorite activities as burdensome, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame "mostly at night" and replaying events, fitting "some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily, pervasive, uncontrollable worry with physical anxiety symptoms, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete episodes of unexpected fear with physical symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness), consistent with panic attacks occurring "a couple of times" = "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She reports struggling "most days" and feeling "barely one step ahead," matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple nights of difficulty sleeping due to racing thoughts and emotional distress, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent daily sadness in waves, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score ≥14 with clear functional impairment meets EPDS criteria for probable <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Patient endorses ≥5 DSM-5 criteria: depressed mood most days, diminished interest/pleasure, fatigue, guilt/self-blame, sleep disturbance, psychomotor agitation (panic episodes), and concentration difficulty. Symptoms began postpartum, cause clinically significant distress, and are not attributable to substances or medical conditions; no self-harm ideation reported. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> for diagnostic confirmation and treatment planning
2. Consider same-day referral to <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> or psychiatry
3. Discuss starting evidence-based psychotherapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy)
4. Provide immediate <med>postpartum support group</med> and local hotline numbers
5. Encourage 15-20 min daily sunlight walk and acceptance of household help to improve sleep
6. Supply written emergency plan: call 988 or local ED if thoughts of self-harm develop
7. Re-screen with EPDS in 1-2 weeks to track symptom trajectory
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]  
Clinician: [licensed MHP]  
Source: self-report on EPDS-10 analog

Symptoms endorsed  
- Marked anhedonia (Q2) and blunted capacity for pleasure (Q1)  
- Persistent, unexplained anxiety/panic episodes (Q4, Q5)  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt when infant fusses (Q3)  
- Overwhelm with daily infant care, sense of barely coping (Q6)  
- Mood-congruent initial insomnia (Q7)  
- Sad/miserable affect most days (Q8)  
- Subjective tearfulness without overt crying (Q9)  
- Denies any self-harm ideation (Q10)

Pattern  
Consistent picture of low mood, loss of enjoyment, prominent anxiety and ruminative guilt, all emerging since delivery. No psychotic features or suicidal thoughts reported.

Screening significance  
Responses place patient above standard cut-off for probable major or minor postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; functional impairment evident (sleep disruption, difficulty anticipating daily tasks).

Risk factors  
- Primiparous, early postpartum period  
- Infant night-waking as primary trigger for rumination and panic-equivalent symptoms  
- No social comparison buffer (“other moms look put-together”)  
- Absence of personal/family psychiatric hx per this encounter  
- Protective factor: strong infant attachment, no self-harm intent

Recommendation  
Score indicates need for formal diagnostic interview and consideration of stepped-care plan (supportive counseling, psycho-education, possible pharmacologic consult). Provide immediate safety resources; reassess in 1–2 weeks or sooner if symptoms escalate.
